implementation_notes: Rust's sprawl is at least honest about its cost: each service is a statically linked binary, so N services means N copies of the runtime and N CVE surfaces, and a shared library update is N workspace bumps and N rebuilds. The `cargo workspace` is the natural place to consolidate — many crates, one binary — and it keeps compile-time boundaries while removing the deployment ones, which is the same trade as the modular monolith. The detection is the workspace member list and the container registry. Rust's specific accelerant is that a workspace makes it easy to run each member as its own binary, which is convenient locally and becomes sprawl in production.
idiom_name: one cargo binary per capability; workspace without a shared deployment
pitfalls: N statically linked binaries means N copies of the standard library and N CVE surfaces for the same version.
A workspace makes per-member deployment so convenient that the default becomes sprawl unless the packaging is decided deliberately.
Shared types across crates mean a schema change ripples through the workspace even when only one service should have changed.
